Bridge linking Poland to Germany is now a barrier against migrants

The town of Slubice respects open borders, but not if you are a Syrian refugee

The twinned towns of Germany’s Frankfurt an der Oder and Poland’s Slubice, neighbouring places separated only by a meandering stretch of the Oder river, have a motto: No borders.

That is, unless you happen to be a Syrian refugee.

At the Polish end of the bridge that connects the two cities, a pair of policemen look for refugees coming over from Germany, scanning the faces of those crossing on foot, on bicycles and inside vehicles.

“They permanently monitor the area around the bridge and check people of specific looks, and check if they have the right to cross to the Polish side. And these people know now that they cannot simply come here,” Tomasz Ciszewicz, mayor of Slubice, told the Financial Times.

He monitors people crossing the bridge through a camera connected to his desk computer.

Poland treasures the open borders and free movement enshrined by its 2004 EU membership. Cross-border trade, particularly with Germany, has been the lifeblood of its robust economy while its citizens have gone in droves to the UK to find better paying jobs and education.

But Slubice, with its makeshift border guards and racial profiling, shows the depth of public opposition to, and even fear of, migrants in Poland.

That sentiment helps to explain Polish politicians’ intransigence on the issue, and how the country has emerged as a chief obstacle to Brussels and Berlin as they try to implement EU-wide policies to share migrants more evenly across Europe.

“We hear a lot of things here about the refugees, [like] that they accost girls in Frankfurt,” said Justyna, a 34-year-old trader selling clothes in the town’s market. “Of course I am worried that if they were relocated here, on this side of the river, and I would go out in the evening, I would think that I could be approached.”

Before Poland joined the EU, a border post on Slubice’s bridge represented a barrier to the west — but since then the end of passport checks and long queues has become a source of pride.

Freedom of movement is the lifeblood of the city, with freight trucks filling the roads and shoppers speaking both Polish and German thronging cut-price cigarette shops.

The approach by Germany and Poland to the European migration crisis could not be more opposed. More than 1m migrants and refugees from the Middle East and Africa have arrived in Germany since the start of 2015. Berlin has championed an EU plan to share refugees between member states to ease the burden on Greece and Italy, where the overwhelming majority enter the continent. SLUBICE, POLAND - APRIL 16: German visitors shop for cigarettes that are cheaper than in Germany at an outdoor market near the German-Polish border on April 16, 2014 in Slubice, Poland. May 1 will mark ten years since the European Union expanded east, taking in countries like Poland, the Czech Republic and the Baltic states as new members. And though the border region between Germany and Poland is flourishing with trade and cultural exchange, the open border has also brought a sharp rise in crime, especially car theft, in communities in Germany close to Poland.

By contrast, Poland’s rightwing government has made it clear that newcomers are not welcome. Warsaw has refused to support the EU’s relocation programme, and it is resisting the arrival of the first batch of 7,000 refugees that the previous administration agreed to relocate — with the support of 70 per cent of its public, according to a poll this month.

This closed-door stance has been condemned by some European politicians as a rejection of the EU’s liberal values. It has also become one of the most striking effects of Poland’s change of government, after a landslide victory in October ushered in the broadly nationalist and Eurosceptic Law and Justice party after eight years of a liberal centre-right government.

“Those people are crossing the border, without being registered, with no legal status. [They] could commit a crime and we would not be able to find them,” said Mr Ciszewicz.

He has used city funds to borrow extra policemen from a nearby town to patrol the bridge, after citizens told him of their fears of refugees carrying out “terrorist attacks”.

Mr Ciszewicz says refugees granted residency in Germany have no legal right to enter Poland. EU rules forbid refugees from working or permanently relocating to another country, but refugees with official protected status from a member state are allowed to make temporary visits to other member states.

Border spot checks are permitted under the EU’s Schengen open-borders agreement if countries notify Brussels, but racial profiling by border officers is banned. About 1,150 refugees with German residency have been housed in and around Frankfurt an der Oder.

Poland’s government — in conjunction with central European allies in Hungary, the Czech Republic and Slovakia — has not only refused to sign up to the EU’s relocation plan, but has actively sought to repeal it.

“I cannot see a possibility to implement this [relocation system] . . . it is dead,” Konrad Szymanski, Poland’s Europe minister, told Polish daily Dziennik Gazeta Prawna last week.

The EU is struggling to respond to a surge of desperate migrants that has resulted in thousands of deaths

Poland’s Office of Foreigners, the executive body responsible for admitting refugees, says the transfer agreed by the last administration may never take place and suggests that Greek and Italian officials were at fault for not processing refugees’ relocation requests.

Poland is the EU’s most homogenous country and about 90 per cent of its citizens are Catholic. There are small pockets of immigrants, such as culturally similar Ukrainians in cities across the country and a well-integrated Vietnamese population in the capital Warsaw.

“If those people want to co-operate, if they respect our culture, if they do not isolate and if they spend money here, they are welcome,” said Mr Ciszewicz. “But if they want to come here in groups, want to attack someone or provoke someone or behave in an inappropriate way, we will not tolerate that.”
